slides.body: Welcome back to Git and GitHub Deep Mastery.
The textbook's framing: everything in this part except the repository content is GitHub Actions, a service that reacts to events on GitHub by running commands on machines.
This video does two things. It gives you the model: seven terms and which contains which.
One statement about evidence, which holds for all of Part 6. Nothing in these chapters was run on GitHub by the authors.
Here's what you'll walk away with.

EVENT ----------------> starts one RUN of each workflow whose trigger matches
   (push, pull request,
    schedule, manual)

   +-- WORKFLOW: a file in .github/workflows/ on a commit -------------------------+
   |                                                                               |
   |  +-- RUN (run ID, run number, attempt) -----------------------------------+   |
   |  |                                                                        |   |
   |  |  +-- JOB build -------------------+      +-- JOB report -----------+   |   |
   |  |  | RUNNER: a new VM               |      | RUNNER: another new VM  |   |   |
   |  |  |                                |      | (needs: build)          |   |   |
   |  |  |  STEP 1  uses: an ACTION       |      |                         |   |   |
   |  |  |  STEP 2  run:  a SHELL process | ---> |  STEP 1  run: a SHELL   |   |   |
   |  |  |  STEP 3  uses: an ACTION       | job  |          process        |   |   |
   |  |  |  STEP 4  run:  a SHELL process | outputs                        |   |   |
   |  |  +--------------------------------+ (strings) ---------------------+   |   |

slides.headline: Step 5: a tab
slides.body: You copy the sample project, add workflow 1, commit, and create the repository with gh repo create and --push.
Five mistakes to watch for.

items: An unquoted version such as 3.10 in a matrix. Root cause: an unquoted scalar is typed by its shape, and as a number it is 3.1.
A multi-line script under >. Root cause: the folded form joins the lines with spaces, so two commands become one wrong command, without an error.
A custom tool that looks for the key on after loading the file with a YAML 1.1 parser. Root cause: that parser reads on as the boolean true.
Expecting a file or an installed tool from one job in the next. Root cause: a job is the unit of isolation and runs on a fresh machine.
Reading the test command first and the trigger last. Root cause: whether a run exists, and for which commit, is decided before any step runs.
An unquoted version such as 3.10 in a matrix. Root cause: an unquoted scalar is typed by its shape, and as a number it is 3.1.
A multi-line script under >. Root cause: the folded form joins the lines with spaces, so two commands become one wrong command, without an error.

Today you learned the seven terms of the Actions model, and you caught YAML changing a value without an error.

beats.text: Four questions a CTO can ask about one pull request, a proposal on GitHub to merge one branch into another. "The tests passed on your laptop and failed in CI on the same commit. Was it the same commit?" "The build stamped the release with a commit ID and not with a version. Who removed the tags?"
beats.tele: Four questions a CTO can ask about one pull request, a proposal on GitHub to merge one branch into another. "The tests passed on your laptop and failed in CI on the same commit. Was it the same commit?" "The build stamped the release with a commit ID and not with a version. Who removed the tags?"

beats.text: "This workflow has a paths filter and is a required check. Why is the pull request waiting forever?" "The job is green. Did the tests run, or did a pipe swallow the failure?" CI, by the way, is the automated checking of each change.
beats.tele: "This workflow has a `paths` filter and is a required check. Why is the pull request waiting forever?" "The job is green. Did the tests run, or did a pipe swallow the failure?" CI, by the way, is the automated checking of each change.

beats.text: The chapter makes a claim about these four, and it's the claim of this whole part of the course: none of them is answered by knowing YAML keys. Each is answered by knowing what a runner, the machine that runs your job, has on disk and in its environment when your command starts.
beats.tele: The chapter makes a claim about these four, and it's the claim of this whole part of the course: none of them is answered by knowing YAML keys. Each is answered by knowing what a runner, the machine that runs your job, has on disk and in its environment when your command starts.

beats.text: Welcome back to Git and GitHub Deep Mastery. Pull up a chair, and welcome to Part 6. So far the course has been about Git and about GitHub as a platform. From here on there's a third layer, and you'll see its lower-third label often.
beats.tele: Welcome back to Git and GitHub Deep Mastery. Pull up a chair, and welcome to Part 6. So far the course has been about Git and about GitHub as a platform. From here on there's a third layer, and you'll see its lower-third label often.

beats.text: The textbook's framing: everything in this part except the repository content is GitHub Actions, a service that reacts to events on GitHub by running commands on machines. Git appears in exactly one place, when a job fetches commits onto the runner. That place causes most of the surprises, and it has its own video, video 145.

Git appears in exactly one place, when a job fetches commits onto the runner. That place causes most of the surprises, and it has its own video, video 145.

beats.text: This video does two things. It gives you the model: seven terms and which contains which. And it teaches you to read YAML, the indented text format that workflow files are written in, as data, because a workflow file is parsed before GitHub Actions interprets a single key.

The workflow files of the course were parse-checked and assembled from documented syntax and from each action's own definition at the pinned version. They weren't executed on GitHub by the author. The labs have you run them. So when a workflow fails for a reason the authors couldn't test, that's material for diagnosis and not a defect in your setup.

beats.tele: After this video you can:

beats.tele: define workflow, event, job, step, action, runner and shell and say which contains which;

beats.text: read a workflow file in a fixed order to predict when it runs, where, and with what;
beats.tele: read a workflow file in a fixed order to predict when it runs, where, and with what;

beats.text: name the YAML features that change the meaning of a workflow without an error;
beats.tele: name the YAML features that change the meaning of a workflow without an error;

beats.text: explain why the key on needs care and what a tab does;
beats.tele: explain why the key `on` needs care and what a tab does;

beats.text: In one sentence. A workflow is a YAML file in the repository that says "when this event happens, run these jobs". Each job is a list of steps that run in order on one fresh machine called a runner. A step is either a shell command or an action, which is a packaged program.
beats.tele: In one sentence. A workflow is a YAML file in the repository that says "when this event happens, run these jobs". Each job is a list of steps that run in order on one fresh machine called a runner. A step is either a shell command or an action, which is a packaged program.

beats.text: Precisely. The terms, as the workflow syntax reference uses them.
beats.tele: Precisely. The terms, as the workflow syntax reference uses them.

beats.text: A workflow is a configurable automated process defined by a YAML file. The file must be in .github/workflows and end in .yml or .yaml.
beats.tele: A workflow is a configurable automated process defined by a YAML file. The file must be in `.github/workflows` and end in `.yml` or `.yaml`.

beats.text: An event is an activity on GitHub, such as a push, a pull request activity or a release. Or a schedule. Or a manual or API request. An event isn't written anywhere. It happens.
beats.tele: An event is an activity on GitHub, such as a push, a pull request activity or a release. Or a schedule. Or a manual or API request. An event isn't written anywhere. It happens.

beats.text: The trigger is the on key of a workflow: which events, with which filters, start a run.
beats.tele: The trigger is the `on` key of a workflow: which events, with which filters, start a run.

beats.text: A workflow run is one execution of a workflow for one event. It has a run ID, a run number and, when re-run, an attempt number.
beats.tele: A workflow run is one execution of a workflow for one event. It has a run ID, a run number and, when re-run, an attempt number.

beats.text: A job is a set of steps that execute on the same runner. Jobs of one run execute in parallel unless needs orders them.
beats.tele: A job is a set of steps that execute on the same runner. Jobs of one run execute in parallel unless `needs` orders them.

beats.text: A step is one run command line or script, or one uses reference to an action. Steps of a job execute in order.
beats.tele: A step is one `run` command line or script, or one `uses` reference to an action. Steps of a job execute in order.

beats.text: An action is a reusable program referenced by uses, with an owner, a repository and a ref. It's a JavaScript program, a composite of steps, or a Docker container, declared by the action.yml in its repository.
beats.tele: An action is a reusable program referenced by `uses`, with an owner, a repository and a ref. It's a JavaScript program, a composite of steps, or a Docker container, declared by the `action.yml` in its repository.

beats.text: A runner is the machine that executes one job. A GitHub-hosted runner is a new virtual machine per job, chosen by runs-on.
beats.tele: A runner is the machine that executes one job. A GitHub-hosted runner is a new virtual machine per job, chosen by `runs-on`.

beats.text: And the shell is the program that executes a run step. Each run step is a new process.
beats.tele: And the shell is the program that executes a `run` step. Each `run` step is a new process.

beats.text: Three properties follow from those definitions, and they explain most of what the next videos show.
beats.tele: Three properties follow from those definitions, and they explain most of what the next videos show.

beats.text: First: a job is the unit of isolation. A job starts on a fresh machine. Files, installed tools and environment variables don't carry from job to job. Data crosses jobs only as job outputs, which are strings. As artifacts, which are files. Or as caches, which are files on a best-effort basis.
beats.tele: First: a job is the unit of isolation. A job starts on a fresh machine. Files, installed tools and environment variables don't carry from job to job. Data crosses jobs only as job outputs, which are strings. As artifacts, which are files. Or as caches, which are files on a best-effort basis.

beats.text: Quick quiz. Step one of a job runs cd src. Step two runs ls. Where does step two start? A, inside src. B, back where step one started. Your answer?
beats.tele: Quick quiz. Step one of a job runs `cd src`. Step two runs `ls`. Where does step two start? A, inside `src`. B, back where step one started. Your answer?

beats.text: B. Second: a step is the unit of process. Steps of one job share the filesystem of the runner, but each run step is a new shell process. A cd or an export in one step is gone in the next.
beats.tele: B. Second: a step is the unit of process. Steps of one job share the filesystem of the runner, but each `run` step is a new shell process. A `cd` or an `export` in one step is gone in the next.

says: Each run step is a new shell process: a cd or an export is gone in the next

beats.text: Third: the workflow file is versioned with the code. For push and pull_request the workflow definition is read from the commit the event refers to, so a branch can change its own CI. For several other events it is read from the default branch only.
beats.tele: Third: the workflow file is versioned with the code. For `push` and `pull_request` the workflow definition is read from the commit the event refers to, so a branch can change its own CI. For several other events it is read from the default branch only.

beats.text: Inside .git. A workflow is an ordinary blob, the object that holds the bytes of one file, at a path under .github/workflows/ in a commit's tree. Nothing else in the repository's Git data describes Actions. Runs, jobs, logs, artifacts, caches, secrets and variables are GitHub objects. A clone doesn't contain them, and git log can't show them.
beats.tele: Inside `.git`. A workflow is an ordinary blob, the object that holds the bytes of one file, at a path under `.github/workflows/` in a commit's tree. Nothing else in the repository's Git data describes Actions. Runs, jobs, logs, artifacts, caches, secrets and variables are GitHub objects. A clone doesn't contain them, and `git log` can't show them.

beats.text: YAML. In one sentence: a workflow file is data, not a script. A YAML parser turns it into nested maps, lists and scalars before GitHub Actions interprets any key, so indentation and quoting decide what GitHub sees.
beats.tele: YAML. In one sentence: a workflow file is data, not a script. A YAML parser turns it into nested maps, lists and scalars before GitHub Actions interprets any key, so indentation and quoting decide what GitHub sees.

beats.text: Four rules cover the mistakes that occur in workflow files.
beats.tele: Four rules cover the mistakes that occur in workflow files.

beats.text: One. Indentation is structure, and tabs aren't indentation. A key belongs to the map whose column it sits in. A tab character in indentation is a syntax error.
beats.tele: One. Indentation is structure, and tabs aren't indentation. A key belongs to the map whose column it sits in. A tab character in indentation is a syntax error.

beats.text: Two. An unquoted scalar is typed by its shape. 3.10 without quotes is a number, and the number is 3.1. v1.0 is a string because of the v. So quote everything that's a version, a label or a glob. The filter pattern cheat sheet adds that patterns starting with a star, a square bracket or an exclamation mark must be quoted, because those characters are YAML syntax.
beats.tele: Two. An unquoted scalar is typed by its shape. `3.10` without quotes is a number, and the number is 3.1. `v1.0` is a string because of the `v`. So quote everything that's a version, a label or a glob. The filter pattern cheat sheet adds that patterns starting with a star, a square bracket or an exclamation mark must be quoted, because those characters are YAML syntax.

beats.text: Three. The vertical bar keeps line breaks. The greater-than sign folds them into spaces. A multi-line run script needs the bar.
beats.tele: Three. The vertical bar keeps line breaks. The greater-than sign folds them into spaces. A multi-line `run` script needs the bar.

beats.text: Four. An ampersand with a name marks a node, and a star with the name reuses it. Anchors and aliases are standard YAML and have been accepted in workflow files since the eighteenth of September 2025.
beats.tele: Four. An ampersand with a name marks a node, and a star with the name reuses it. Anchors and aliases are standard YAML and have been accepted in workflow files since the eighteenth of September 2025.

beats.text: Analogy. A workflow is a standing order at a print shop: "Whenever a manuscript arrives, give one copy to the proofreader and one to the typesetter, each at a clean desk, each following a numbered checklist, some items of which say 'use the house stamping machine'." The manuscript arriving is the event. The two workers are two jobs. The clean desk is the runner. The checklist is the steps. The stamping machine is an action.
beats.tele: Analogy. A workflow is a standing order at a print shop: "Whenever a manuscript arrives, give one copy to the proofreader and one to the typesetter, each at a clean desk, each following a numbered checklist, some items of which say 'use the house stamping machine'." The manuscript arriving is the event. The two workers are two jobs. The clean desk is the runner. The checklist is the steps. The stamping machine is an action.

beats.text: The textbook says the analogy breaks in two places. The desks are destroyed after each job, so nothing left on one is found by the next. And the manuscript isn't handed over: the worker must fetch it, and by default fetches only the last page.
beats.tele: The textbook says the analogy breaks in two places. The desks are destroyed after each job, so nothing left on one is found by the next. And the manuscript isn't handed over: the worker must fetch it, and by default fetches only the last page.

beats.text: Hold on to "only the last page". It's the shallow checkout, and it answers the CTO's second question.
beats.tele: Hold on to "only the last page". It's the shallow checkout, and it answers the CTO's second question.

beats.text: A reading order. The textbook explains workflow 1 from top to bottom: name, trigger, permissions, job and runner, then the steps. This course uses that as a fixed order for every workflow file you meet, and you'll use it in the gate.
beats.tele: A reading order. The textbook explains workflow 1 from top to bottom: name, trigger, permissions, job and runner, then the steps. This course uses that as a fixed order for every workflow file you meet, and you'll use it in the gate.

beats.text: First, the trigger. Which events, with which filters? That tells you when a run exists at all, and for which commit and ref.
beats.tele: First, the trigger. Which events, with which filters? That tells you when a run exists at all, and for which commit and ref.

beats.text: Second, the permissions. What may the job's token, the credential it uses to call GitHub, do?
beats.tele: Second, the permissions. What may the job's token, the credential it uses to call GitHub, do?

beats.text: Third, each job: on which runner, after which other jobs, under which conditions.
beats.tele: Third, each job: on which runner, after which other jobs, under which conditions.

beats.text: Fourth, the first steps of the job: what's checked out, and how much of it.
beats.tele: Fourth, the first steps of the job: what's checked out, and how much of it.

beats.text: Fifth and last, the commands that are the real check.
beats.tele: Fifth and last, the commands that are the real check.

beats.text: People read in the opposite order. They go to the test command first because it's familiar. But a correct test command that runs on the wrong commit, or never runs, proves nothing.
beats.tele: People read in the opposite order. They go to the test command first because it's familiar. But a correct test command that runs on the wrong commit, or never runs, proves nothing.

beats.text: Read it from the outside in. An event starts a run. The run holds two jobs, each on its own new machine. Inside a job, every step is an action or a shell process. And between build and report, only job outputs cross, and those are strings.
beats.tele: Read it from the outside in. An event starts a run. The run holds two jobs, each on its own new machine. Inside a job, every step is an action or a shell process. And between `build` and `report`, only job outputs cross, and those are strings.

beats.text: The second element is 3.1. There's the puzzle from the opening. A matrix, a list of variants that each get their own job, written with unquoted 3.10 asks for Python 3.1. This is a property of numbers, not of one parser. The quoted one stayed a string. yes and NO became booleans, because YAML 1.1 says so.

beats.text: Step 2: the key on.
beats.tele: Step 2: the key `on`.
